problem: There is no simulator for learning-based ground-robot navigation in outdoor unstructured terrain that combines photorealism, real-time agent interaction and automatic scene variability. CARLA models urban scenes with static hand-crafted maps. AirSim ships no scenes. Habitat, AI2-THOR and House3D are indoor. OAISYS (Blender) cannot run real-time interaction. Flightmare targets aerial vehicles.
motivation: Robots in forests, planetary surfaces, search-and-rescue sites and fields face highly variable, cluttered scenes, and collecting real-world training data there is costly, risky and low in variety. In unstructured outdoor settings the variability comes from the scene itself, not from traffic or pedestrians. So procedural scene generation with controllable difficulty is seen as the key to training policies that generalize.
key_idea: MIDGARD is an Unreal-Engine-based, Gym-compatible simulator that procedurally generates photorealistic unstructured outdoor scenes. Scene descriptors place objects on a grid of cells, each filled with probability equal to a user-set difficulty D, so obstacle density and therefore navigation difficulty can be controlled.
insight: The difficulty knob D (obstacle density) directly and monotonically lowers RL navigation performance. For SAC in Forest at 10 m, SR falls from 62% to 51% to 37% as D goes 0.1→0.5→1.0; larger start-goal distance (20 m) lowers SR further. This supports using the generator for controlled difficulty and curriculum learning. Off-policy discrete SAC beats PPO in every reported setting, and the gap widens with difficulty and distance (e.g., Forest D=1.0, 20 m: 27% vs 15%). The evaluation does not test generalization to held-out scenes or sim-to-real transfer.
method: Scene descriptors + procedural generation: a scene type has a base map, a min/max grid cell size (C_min, C_max) and placeable world objects. Each object has a mesh, a min/max size, a max tilt from the ground normal and a max ground slope for placement. Cell size is C = C_min + G_res(C_max − C_min). In each cell an object is placed at a random location with probability D (difficulty in [0,1]) if the slope constraint allows. Generating a scene takes about 1 s.

Pre-built scene types: Meadow (easy-medium, grass, non-traversable lake), Forest (medium-high, trees/rocks/branches/puddles), Volcanic field (medium-high, flat-colored rocky uneven terrain) and Arctic glacier (high difficulty, snow-covered rocks and ice with low contrast). New descriptors can be authored in Unreal.

Perception module: configurable cameras (FoV, pose, resolution 128–1024) producing RGB, depth, and instance/semantic segmentation with classes ground, bush, tree, rock, water, debris, artificial. Low-level sensors: GPS-like pose, target location, IMU (attitude/speed/acceleration) and collision detection.

Control suite: two 4-wheel vehicles, either discrete (brake, forward, backward, turn left, turn right) or continuous (brake, linear speed, angular speed). Actions persist until a new one arrives, so agent and environment run asynchronously.

Engine and API: render quality Low–Cinematic, multiple cameras, configurable map size and simulated time per step. OpenAI Gym Python interface; C++/Blueprint feature extension; Blueprint functions exposed as HTTP endpoints. About 120 sim steps/s at High quality and about 60 FPS frame capture at High, 512×512, 1 camera.

Reference RL agent for point-goal navigation: an MS-COCO-pretrained DeepLabV3 encoder gives an 8×8×960 map, adaptive max-pooled into FC layers (128, 64, 64). A state branch (normalized distance, heading, distance delta) uses 2 FC layers of 64. The concatenated features go through FC layers (128, 64, 64, 5 actions). Trained with PPO and discrete SAC for 20,000 episodes.

Reward and episodes: +10 on reaching the target, −10 on collision or crossing non-traversable terrain, −0.05 per step, −0.1 when moving away from the target. Episodes are capped at 500 steps, with 100 ms simulated per step and discount 0.99.

setting.backbone: DeepLabV3 encoder (MS-COCO pretrained) + MLP policy, trained with PPO and discrete SAC (reference baselines; the paper's contribution is the simulator)
setting.training_data: 20,000 RL episodes per setting in procedurally generated MIDGARD scenes (Forest / Volcanic field) at a given difficulty D and target distance
setting.observation: monocular RGB 256×256 (camera 1 m above ground, tilted 10° down, 90° FoV) + GPS-derived normalized distance and heading to goal + change in distance between steps
setting.action_space: discrete 5 actions: brake, forward, backward, turn left, turn right (a continuous brake/linear/angular-speed vehicle is also available)
setting.privileged: goal position known (GPS-like distance/heading to target, standard point-goal setting); none otherwise

numbers_note: This is a simulator paper. The only navigation results are the authors' PPO/SAC reference agents on their own MIDGARD point-goal task, with no official train/test split and no stated separation between training and evaluation scenes. The metric keys encode difficulty D and start-target distance. The Volcanic SAC rewards are printed with comma decimal separators ('-2,73', '-5,48', …) and are transcribed here as decimals. Simulator frame-capture FPS (Table I, e.g. 60 FPS at High/512/1 camera; 110 FPS at Low/128/1 camera) is not included in numbers. No variance or number of seeds is reported.
results: On MIDGARD point-goal navigation, discrete SAC reaches up to 62% SR (Forest, D=0.1, 10 m) and 60% (Volcanic, D=0.1, 10 m), with PPO at 54% and 48% respectively. Both degrade sharply with obstacle density and distance, down to 27%/22% for SAC and 15%/15% for PPO at D=1.0, 20 m. SAC beats PPO in every setting. The platform delivers about 60 FPS frame capture at High quality, 512×512, one camera, and generates a scene in about 1 s. Its feature comparison against AirSim, Habitat and CARLA stresses that only MIDGARD offers procedural, difficulty-controllable scenes.
limitations: Only a single agent per scene, a single 4-wheel robot model family, and simplified agent-terrain interaction physics; no ROS bridge yet (all stated as future work).
Evaluation is thin: two RL baselines on two scenes, no held-out-scene generalization test, no sim-to-real validation, and no seeds or variance reported.
Assets can only be imported at build time (Unreal); the comparison table's claims about other simulators (e.g., photorealism, frame capture rate) are qualitative or unverified.
